title: The Word Is Near: Faith, Confession, and Sending
summary: Paul prays for Israel's salvation and explains that zeal for God without knowledge led many to pursue their own righteousness instead of submitting to God's. Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, and the word of faith is near: whoever confesses Jesus as Lord and believes God raised him will be saved, Jew and Gentile alike. The chapter traces how people come to believe through preaching and hearing, and it shows from Scripture that Israel heard but did not respond, while God held out his hands to them all day long.
story: Chapter 9 explained Israel's stumbling in terms of God's free mercy and ended by saying Israel pursued righteousness by works rather than by faith. Chapter 10 turns to the human side of the same story. It is full of calling, confessing, believing, hearing, preaching, and sending, and it places responsibility on Israel for not believing the message it heard. Paul holds both sides together without resolving the tension into one of them. The chapter also broadens the view to the Gentile mission, because the same Lord is Lord of all, and prepares for chapter 11's question whether God has rejected his people.
historical:
By the time Paul wrote Romans, around AD 57, the message about Jesus had been preached in synagogues from Judea to Greece for over two decades. Paul himself had usually begun his work in a city at the synagogue (Acts 13:5; 17:1-2; 18:4), so he knew firsthand both the Jews who believed and the many who did not. His description of Israel's zeal in verse 2 reflects his own past. In Galatians 1:14 and Philippians 3:6 he describes himself as extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers and, as to zeal, a persecutor of the church. He speaks of Israel's zeal without contempt, as someone who had shared it.

The phrase "Jesus is Lord" in verse 9 is one of the earliest Christian confessions. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint, made by Jews in the centuries before Jesus), "Lord" (kyrios) regularly stands for God's personal name. In the Roman world, kyrios was also used of the emperor. To confess Jesus as Lord therefore carried both a claim about his identity with Israel's God and an implicit statement of ultimate allegiance.
cultural:
In the ancient world, news traveled by messengers. A herald or runner brought word of a victory or a new ruler, and the arrival of such a messenger was itself an event. Paul quotes Isaiah 52:7 about the beauty of the feet of those who bring good news, a verse that in Isaiah pictures messengers running across the hills to announce that Israel's God reigns and the exile is ending. The Greek word for good news, euangelion, was also used for public announcements such as the birth or accession of an emperor. Paul's chain of questions in verses 14 and 15 assumes this world: people cannot call on someone they have not heard of, and they cannot hear unless someone is sent.

Confession "with your mouth" and belief "in your heart" reflect Hebrew thinking, in which the heart is the center of thought, will, and loyalty, not only of emotion. Public confession mattered in a culture of honor and shame. To say aloud that a crucified Jew was Lord could cost a person family, trade, and standing.
literary: Romans 10 is built as a close reading of Scripture. Paul contrasts two voices: the righteousness that is by the law, speaking in Leviticus 18:5, and the righteousness that is by faith, which he lets speak in the words of Deuteronomy 30:12-14. He interprets the Deuteronomy passage phrase by phrase, adding comments in the style of Jewish commentary ("that is, to bring Christ down"). Verses 14 and 15 form a chain of questions that runs backward from calling on the Lord to believing, hearing, preaching, and being sent. The last section (verses 16-21) strings together quotations from Isaiah, the Psalms, and Deuteronomy to answer two objections: that Israel did not hear, and that Israel did not understand. The chapter ends not with a conclusion but with God's outstretched hands.

outline.t: Zeal without knowledge and Christ the end of the law
The word of faith is near: confess and believe
How they will hear: preaching and sending
Israel heard, and God still holds out his hands

doctrines.note: Verses 9 to 13 give one of the clearest statements of how a person is saved: by believing in the heart that God raised Jesus from the dead and confessing with the mouth that Jesus is Lord. The promise is universal: everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.

The chain in verses 14 and 15 makes the sending of messengers part of God's way of saving. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ, so the preaching of the gospel is not an optional extra but the means God uses.

Faith in this chapter is trust in what God has done in raising Jesus, expressed in confession. It is set against establishing one's own righteousness. Faith receives a righteousness that comes from God.

words.note: Telos, end, goal, or completion. In verse 4 Christ is the telos of the law. Readers debate whether Paul means the end as termination (the law's era as a way to righteousness is over), goal (the law pointed to Christ all along), or both. Many interpreters think both senses are present: the law was heading toward Christ, and with his coming its role as the boundary of God's people has reached its end.

Homologeo, to confess or acknowledge publicly, literally to say the same thing. It was used for agreeing to terms and for public declarations. In verses 9 and 10 it is the open, spoken acknowledgment of Jesus as Lord, the counterpart of inward belief. Paul does not set the two against each other; they are two sides of one response.

Akoe, hearing, report, or message heard. In verse 16 it translates Isaiah's question about who has believed the report, and in verse 17 it describes how faith comes. The word can mean both the act of hearing and the message itself, which suits Paul's point that faith depends on a message that has actually been spoken and heard.

christ: This chapter shows Christ as the one in whom God's righteousness is given to all who believe. Paul applies to Jesus the words of Joel 2:32, "Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved". In Joel, "the Lord" is the God of Israel; Paul identifies Jesus as the Lord on whom people now call, a striking sign of how the earliest Christians understood him. The reading of Deuteronomy 30 also points to Christ: no one needs to ascend to heaven to bring him down or descend to the deep to bring him up, because God has already sent him and raised him. The message is near, and it is about Christ himself. The resurrection stands at the center of saving faith (verse 9), which fits Paul's statement in 4:25 that Jesus was raised for our justification.

hard.q: If faith comes by hearing, what about those who have never heard of Christ?
hard.a:
Verses 14 and 15 are among the texts Christians use when they ask about those who die without hearing the gospel, and the church has answered in more than one way. Some, often called exclusivists or restrictivists, read this chapter as teaching that explicit faith in Christ is necessary for salvation, which gives urgency to mission. Others, often called inclusivists, hold that salvation is only through Christ but that God may save some who respond in faith to what they know of him, pointing to figures like Melchizedek and Job and to Romans 2:14-16. A further view holds that people who never heard will have an opportunity at or after death, a position with a smaller following.

Paul's own concern in this chapter is not the fate of those who never heard but the responsibility of Israel, who did hear (verse 18). His quotation of Psalm 19:4, which describes the heavens proclaiming God's glory, applies it to the spread of the gospel. Whatever position a reader takes on the wider question, the chapter's own application is clear: the message must be sent and preached, because God saves through it. Christians agree that salvation is God's work through Christ and that God is just; they differ on how he deals with those beyond the church's reach.

questions: Paul admits Israel had real zeal for God but not according to knowledge. How can sincere religious commitment still miss God's righteousness?
What is the relationship between believing in your heart and confessing with your mouth? Why does Paul insist on both?
The chapter ends with God holding out his hands to a resistant people. What does that image say about how God treats those who refuse him?
